units.label: paragraph 3
units.text: In 1692, a group of young girls in Salem Village, Massachusetts began having seizures and other odd attacks after hearing tales told by a slave. They accused several women of being witches. The townspeople were horrified, but not surprised. Belief in witchcraft was widespread throughout 17th century America and Europe. Town officials called a court to hear the trial.  Within a month, six women were convicted and hanged.

units.label: paragraph 4
units.text: The craze grew, as the court allowed witnesses to testify that they had seen the accused women as spirits or visions in dreams.  This “spectral evidence” could not be verified or proven with hard evidence.  By the fall of 1692, 20 victims, including several men, had been executed and more than 100 others were in jail.  Among them were some of the town’s most important citizens.  When the charges threatened to spread beyond Salem, ministers throughout the colony called for an end to the trials. Those still in jail were later freed of their charges.

units.label: paragraph 5
units.text: Although this was a one-time incident, the Salem trials has always fascinated Americans. Most historians agree that Salem Village in 1692 experienced a kind of public hysteria, fueled by genuine belief in the existence of witchcraft.  While some of the girls may have been acting, many responsible adults became caught up in the situation as well.

units.label: paragraph 6
units.text: Even more revealing is a closer analysis of the identities of the accused and the accusers. Salem Village, like most of Colonial New England, was undergoing an economic and political transition.  They had long been Puritan farmers, but their society was becoming more modern, commercial, and secular. Many of the accusers were representatives of the traditional life of farming and religion, while the accused witches were from the rising commercial class.

units.label: paragraph 7
units.text: The Salem Witch Trials also serve as a lesson of what can happen when people make large, but false, accusations.  Three hundred years later, we still call false accusations against a large number of people a “witch hunt.”

The Trials of Salem
In 1692, a group of young girls in Salem Village, Massachusetts began having  
seizures and other odd attacks after hearing tales told by a slave. They accused  
several women of being witches. The townspeople were horrified, but not surprised.  
Belief in witchcraft was widespread throughout 17th century America and Europe.  
Town officials called a court to hear the trial.  Within a month, six women were  
convicted and hanged.
The craze grew, as the court allowed witnesses to testify that they had seen  
the accused women as spirits or visions in dreams.  This “spectral evidence” could  
not be verified or proven with hard evidence.  By the fall of 1692, 20 victims, including 
several men, had been executed and more than 100 others were in jail.  Among them 
were some of the town’s most important citizens.  When the charges threatened to  
spread beyond Salem, ministers throughout the colony called for an end to the trials. 
Those still in jail were later freed of their charges.
Although this was a one-time incident, the Salem trials has always fascinated  
Americans. Most historians agree that Salem Village in 1692 experienced a kind of  
public hysteria, fueled by genuine belief in the existence of witchcraft.  While some of 
the girls may have been acting, many responsible adults became caught up in the  
situation as well.
Even more revealing is a closer analysis of the identities of the accused and  
the accusers. Salem Village, like most of Colonial New England, was undergoing an  
economic and political transition.  They had long been Puritan farmers, but their  
society was becoming more modern, commercial, and secular. Many of the accusers 
were representatives of the traditional life of farming and religion, while the accused  
witches were from the rising commercial class.  
The Salem Witch Trials also serve as a lesson of what can happen when  
people make large, but false, accusations.  Three hundred years later, we still call  
false accusations against a large number of people a “witch hunt.”
